newsitem.title: UK: BT seen struggling in TV war despite Labour pledge.
newsitem.headline: BT seen struggling in TV war despite Labour pledge.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc will struggle to catch up with its domestic arch-rival Cable and Wireless Plc in a battle to offer multi-channel television services, analysts said on Friday.
The opposition Labour Party confirmed that if it won the election on May 1, it would gradually lift restrictions on phone companies offering entertainment services from 1998.

But while BT has yet to confirm that it will branch out into television services, experts said it would take years for the telephone giant to beef up its network so that it can compete with cable and satellite TV groups.
Nevertheless, BT welcomed the announcement in the Labour Party's business manifesto, which endorses an influential all-party select committee report compiled a couple of years ago.

But a company spokesman said it was too soon to say whether BT would offer television services. "We wouldn't want to say until we have definitely got the clearance to do so and clear time scales," he said.

Labour said it wanted full competition throughout the country, adding that it expected telecoms groups to rapidly develop the high-grade networks necessary for interactive communications across the country.

If, as opinion polls forecast, Labour wins the election, BT will soon be free to plan and start the engineering work needed to upgrade its telephone lines so that they can support multi-channel TV services.
The Cable Communications Association, which represents cable companies, was quick to dismiss the Labour business manifesto as old news.

"Existing government policy calls for a review of the restriction in 2001. The additional effect in cable franchises of the Labour Party policy would be minimal and has previously been accounted for both by the cable industry and by the market," a spokesman said.

With increasing competition in Britain's telecoms market already prompting industry regulator Oftel to relax substantial price caps on BT's telephone charges, analysts also voiced little surprise at Labour's policy.
"We knew that Labour had been thinking along those lines," noted Andrew Harrington, telecoms analyst at stockbrokers Salomon Brothers.

But he added: "It doesn't alter our view, which is that by the time BT is able to offer broadcast services in any meaningful way, the cable companies will have five or six million subscribers across the country."

C&W has managed to circumvent current regulatory restrictions on offering entertainment services by merging its national telephone subsidiary Mercury Communications with three cable television companies in a multi-billion pound deal.

The new company, which will be partially floated in London and New York in the next few weeks, will be Britain's biggest cable company. Analysts value the group, called Cable and Wireless Communications, at between 4.5 and 7.0 billion pounds ($11.3 billion).

Although BT has been trying out a pricey combination of sophisticated computer compression and high speed technology that can support multi-channel TV, the company has not decided on whether, or how, to boost its national telephone network.

Not only do current high prices of installing compression technology mean that BT could only target the top end of the market but, unlike cable lines, the technology also does not allow interactive services, such as home banking and shopping, analysts say.

"We're really talking about (BT offering TV services) when the technology comes down in price sufficiently to be able to offer a competitive service relative to the other providers of multi-channel TV," noted Harrington.
Meanwhile, one threat to cable companies comes from satellite and terrestrial digital television which bypass their delivery methods.

Rupert Murdoch's British Sky Broadcasting Group Plc, with which BT has a marketing agreement, has linked with Granada Group Plc and Carlton Communications Plc to bid for a licence to offer a block of digital terrestrial services.
